Pema's diary, Friday.
Rekha resigned today. She said it kindly: "I don't know what we're building any more."
She's not wrong. In January an investor said everything needs AI, so I made us add an AI study buddy. In March another investor said quick delivery was where the money was, so we started talking to stationery shops about ten-minute delivery. Last month I came back from a coffee and told the team we'd become a marketplace for tutors.
Each time, I was excited. Each time, we dropped the last thing after two or three weeks, before we'd learned whether it worked. The team stopped asking questions in meetings. I thought that meant they agreed.
Now I can't answer one simple question: did any of it work? We never tested anything long enough to know.

Their incubator mentor, Mr Menon, drew two columns. "Forget what you want. Tell me why."
Swati went first. "Because two bigger companies are entering this space. If we're slow, we'll miss the window."
Devika took longer. "Because I've seen founders lose control of their own company after raising. I don't want investors deciding what we build."
Mr Menon underlined two words: window, control. "So one of you is afraid of being too late, and one of being overruled. Those aren't opposites. Can you find money that's fast but doesn't take control?"
They looked at each other properly for the first time that month.

Alejandro and Astrid had started their bike-repair app in Copenhagen as friends, and by spring they were fighting as co-founders. Who could hire the new mechanic? Who had the final say on the app's design? Could Astrid spend on ads without asking?

Spending: each can approve up to a set limit alone; above that, both sign. Disagreements: sleep on it, then check this page. They both signed it and pinned it to the office wall.
Three weeks later, Alejandro wanted to rent a second workshop. He opened his mouth to argue, glanced at the page and saw it was above his limit. "Okay," he said. "Let's talk about it together on Friday."

qa.q: Where was the tour company?
qa.a: In Munnar.

qa.q: How did young Joseph feel after winning the meeting, and later?
qa.a: He probably felt triumphant at first, then regretful when Ravi went quiet and the ideas dried up.

qa.q: Which choice in the story went wrong, and what could have fixed it?
qa.a: Arguing like a lawyer to win; listening to Ravi's ideas, like the student package, could have kept both the price and the partnership healthy.

qa.q: How did Ravi experience losing the debate?
qa.a: Ravi felt dismissed and went quiet, suggesting no new routes or ideas for a whole season.

grounding: It shows a young co-founder winning a pricing argument with collected proof, after which his partner stops sharing ideas and the company loses more than a wrong price would cost.
